front: TC018: What is the minimum viable move?
back: Take whatever you were about to say and cut it in half. Lead with the most important word or sentence. Leave the rest.

front: TC018: What is the core sequence?
back: Cut words in half -> Lead with the point -> Earn elaboration.

front: TC018: What is the field tip?
TC018: What is the strong version of: Three paragraphs of context before the ask?
back: I need X by Y. Context in one sentence below.

front: TC018: What is the strong version of: Five-minute verbal explanation of a simple point?
back: One sentence answer. Pause. Add one piece of context only if needed.

front: TC018: What is the strong version of: Email with no clear structure: all text, no hierarchy?
back: Key point in bold at the top. Brief support below. Clear ask at the end.

front: TC018: What is better than: 'I hope this finds you well. I just wanted to touch base to...'?
TC018: What is better than: 'I sort of think we should maybe possibly consider...'?
TC018: What is better than: A message that wanders to its point the way you wandered to it?
back: Write it all, then send only the destination.

front: TC018: What are signs it is working?
back: People respond faster and more clearly to your communication. You are asked fewer 'so what is the point?' questions. Written communication takes less time to produce and read. Verbal answers land with more impact.

front: TC018: When should you avoid this technique?
back: In relationship-building contexts where brevity reads as cold or dismissive. When explaining complex technical topics to non-experts — completeness matters more than brevity.

front: TC018: What is the best recovery line?
back: 'Ignore my last three sentences; the first one was the point.'
